If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more. Well, according to the transcript, she did say those words. Well, like I said, that wasn't provided to me. Since part one, significant new reporting has emerged. So for now, let's concentrate on what's new. According to the district attorney, her 2024 statement didn't allege gang RAP, but CBS and ABC have since reported more of what she told police. CBS obtained a transcript of her November 2024 interview. According to its reporting, she said, I can say with 100% confidence, I was RAP-ed and described herself as completely and totally incapacitated. She also reportedly described being physically hit very, very hard. The published excerpt doesn't establish who hit her or exactly when. From that interview came the six page statement. She reviewed it, added handwritten notes and signed it. The signature wording said that making a false written statement is a crime. The DA relied on that statement. He says the explicit declaration of RAP wasn't in it and he never saw the transcript and that this changes the landscape. ABC obtained the signed statement itself. It reports that she described the final encounter as feeling like coercion and said she felt unable to make decisions because of her intoxication. She also described being horrified when more men entered. There's also additional context about ketamine. The DA's summary says she took more thinking, why not do it a second time? According to ABC, she said she felt extremely uncomfortable and hoped it might make her pass out. She thought that if men then had sex with her while unconscious, they could be charged with RAP. Those passages were absent from the DA's published summary. He said he selected facts relevant to consent, but being unable to make decisions because of intoxication is hard to see as irrelevant. Some passages also support his interpretation. She reportedly said she was pretty okay with how things started. When asked whether she had said no or said she was tired, she answered, I think it is, I'm tired. But consent to an initial encounter doesn't establish consent to everything that followed. Neither document has been publicly released in full though. We are working with selected excerpts. Now to the messages. In part one, we covered the friendly exchange two days after the night. New reporting shows what followed. ABC obtained October 23rd messages between her and the friend she had come to see. She wrote that rumors were spreading, that her reputation was destroyed, and that she was utterly ashamed. But in the same exchange, she agreed with him that things would get better, wrote that stuff like this is going to become more common, and also wrote, I love you, King. The New York Times describes later messages with the same man about the Halloween party at the fraternity. After the fraternity president disinvited her, she wrote that they weren't her friends and were covering themselves. Then on November 3rd, according to the New York Times, she texted the other man from the first threesome, let's be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. She also wrote that she was given more ketamine than she could remember. On November 7th, ABC shows one of the accused telling her he'd heard he was being labeled an assaulter. She replied that she had warned a friend not to go to Kai Pai, but had never mentioned his name. That same day, according to the Times, she went to an emergency room and asked for an RAPE kit. ABC also quotes a November 7th message from her. In any sexual scenario with one woman and many men, the woman was probably the victim. On November 8th, she cut off contact, saying, I know you liked. The published excerpts don't explain what lie she meant. These messages don't settle content. They show her description of the night shifting over a few weeks, from none of the sexual stuff was illegal to 90% was not consensual. One side may see this as someone coming to terms with what happened. Another side may know the shift came after rumors spread. But either way, the reported messages show she alleged non-consent before going to police. Those who have responded through lawyers denied the allegations. The criminal case has been reopened and Cornell has agreed to an outside review. In another video, I still plan to cover why the lawsuit describes events differently from the DA summary, what Cornell's own investigation found, and why the case is back in the headlines nearly two years later.
